Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Evan had always lived by precision. As a combat pilot, he was used to reading a room quickly, scanning for movement, and trusting trained instincts when situations changed without warning. Before the assault, those habits felt professional and contained. Afterward, they bled into everything. The trauma had occurred during a period when he had let his guard down with someone he believed he could trust, and what stayed with him most was not only the violation itself but the sense that the person had been close enough to be safe. In the months that followed, he found himself returning again and again to that betrayal, convinced that the worst part was that he had not seen it coming. He was single, lived alone, and had to manage the ordinary routines of home and work without the easy reassurance of a partner or family nearby, which made the aftermath feel especially exposed.

Soon after the assault, Evan began noticing how sharply he reacted to uncertainty. Situations that felt ambiguous or unpredictable now set him on edge, whether it was an unexpected knock at the door, an unfamiliar car lingering outside his building, or an interaction in which someone’s behavior seemed slightly off. If a person glanced at him too long in a parking lot or acted in a way he read as suspicious, he found himself watching them closely, tense and ready for something to happen. At home, he did not really settle. Even inside his own apartment he felt on guard, as though the danger could still reach him there. He would pause mid-task to listen, holding still if he thought he heard movement in the hallway, and he became preoccupied with sounds that might mean someone was entering. This vigilance extended into the night. If he woke from a nightmare, the residue of it lingered immediately in his body; he would wake disoriented, heart pounding, and spend the next stretch of time checking the locks and listening for noises before he could even think about going back to sleep.

His startle response also became difficult to ignore. Ordinary sounds that most people would barely register now made him jump — a dropped pan in the kitchen, a sharp bang from somewhere in the building, even a door closing too hard. He described these reactions with embarrassment, as if his body were exposing something weak about him. That sense of weakness fed into the way he talked about himself. Evan had come to believe that his reactions since the assault showed he was a lousy coper, someone who should have been able to handle what happened and move on. He spoke about the event with a kind of self-judgment that seemed to linger just under the surface of everything else. The more he noticed his own fear, the more he saw it as evidence that he had failed in the one way he had always assumed he would not fail: under pressure.

Over time, these reactions began to affect the shape of his daily life. As a pilot, he was required to remain composed in fast-changing environments, yet even outside of work he found himself bracing for the unexpected. He became less willing to stay late at the base if the parking lot felt empty, and at home he developed routines around checking doors and windows before settling in. When he woke from nightmares, he would sit in silence and listen, scanning for signs that someone was there, sometimes for longer than he would have expected himself to need. He did not describe this as a choice so much as a state he could not seem to step out of. The loss of trust ran through all of it. He had lost his faith in people, life, and, at times, something beyond either of those things. The betrayal by someone he had trusted had left him with the sense that ordinary assumptions about safety and decency no longer held. He was not someone who talked easily about vulnerability, but it was clear that the assault had changed what the world felt like to him: less predictable, less reliable, and more dangerous than it had once seemed.

He came for help only after realizing how much energy he was spending staying alert. What brought him in was the exhaustion of being on guard even in his own home, the repeated nightmares that threw him back into vigilance when he woke, and the fear that one day his reactions would become impossible to hide in front of the people he worked with. Beneath that was a quieter hope that he might regain some sense of safety without having to keep listening for danger every hour of the day.
